name: The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders From Mars

info.desc: The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars is the fifth studio album by David Bowie, released on June 16, 1972, through RCA Records. Described as a loose concept album and rock opera, Ziggy Stardust is about Bowie's titular alter ego Ziggy Stardust, a fictional androgynous and bisexual rock star who is sent to Earth as a saviour before an impending apocalyptic disaster. In the story, Ziggy wins the hearts of fans but suffers a fall from grace after succumbing to his own ego. The character was inspired by numerous musicians, including Vince Taylor. Most of .

podcast.body: This album was the major hit Bowie had sought, launching glam rock to prominence. The accompanying tour (January 29, 1972 - July 3, 1973) was rock's most theatrical to date, featuring costume changes, choreography, makeup, tall boots, high platform shoes, and daring sexual ambiguity. "The album, The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and The Spiders from Mars, was the hit he'd been looking for."

podcast.body: Bowie's fifth LP, landing in the spring of 1972, gradually became a sensation by early 1973, fueled by his new alter ego, the orange-haired glam rock alien Ziggy Stardust. This album proved to be Bowie's image-making breakthrough, cracking the UK top 10 and becoming his first album to break into the US Top 100 on the album chart, peaking at number 75 by early 1973. "The Ziggy Stardust LP proved to be David Bowie's image-making breakthrough."

podcast.body: The recording sessions for this seminal album were integral to the conception and development of David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust persona, including the creation of his iconic hairstyle. "The origins of Ziggy's hair is shrouded in legend. podcast.body: This album, released in 1972, was hugely influential and served as Bowie's commercial breakthrough, appealing to glam kids and future punk rock figures. It tells the story of an alien rock star named Ziggy, a name inspired by Bowie's friend Iggy Pop and Texas proto-psychobilly singer Norman O'Dan (The Legendary Stardust Cowboy). The music was originally intended for a full-on musical, stage show, or BBC TV program. The narrative describes a dying Earth five years in the future, with Ziggy initially ignored, then discovering "the Infinite's" (spacemen) who promise salvation, leading Ziggy to believe he is a prophet. Upon the Infinite's arrival, Ziggy dies on stage after contact due to their antimatter composition, after which the now-visible Infinite's absorb his essence. This album dramatically presented rock and roll theatrically with costumes, concept, and playacting, a style previously unseen. "The album tells the story of an alien rock star named Ziggy."

podcast.body: This album, released on June 16, 1972, features one of the most famous album covers of the 1970s, depicting Bowie posing on Heddon Street in London. A conspiracy theory suggests this album cover and its contents predict the rise of Kanye West. "One of the most famous album covers of the 1970s is what we see on the front of Bowie's Ziggy start us in the spiders from Mars album."

podcast.body: This record, released in 1972, is consistently held in higher and higher esteem with each passing year, and is cited as a groundbreaking and influential work in music history. It introduced themes of dystopianism and dread that would be revisited later in his career. "Damn, that's an influential record."

podcast.body: This rock opera was released in the late spring of 1972 and details the story of Ziggy Stardust, an omnisexual rock star sent to Earth five years before its demise due to resource depletion. Ziggy is a messenger from the Starman, tasked with delivering a message of peace and love, but he is ultimately destroyed after believing too much in his own importance as a prophet. The album was added to the National Registry of the Library of Congress in 2016 for its historical and cultural significance. "Ziggy Stardust is an omnisexual rock star who is sent to Earth five years before it dies due to the people of Earth depleting its natural resources."
